data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A rank-22 decomposition of the <3,3,3> tensor exists, but it inherently requires breaking the symmetry group of the tensor, which explains why symmetric tensor decompositions, standard Groebner-basis attacks preserving symmetry, and equivariant ALS searches have systematically failed to find it over the last 47 years.","counterconditions":[{"case":"A rank-22 decomposition that preserves a significant portion of the <3,3,3> symmetry group is discovered.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"An exhaustive search over all asymmetric configurations of 22 rank-1 tensors concludes that no valid decomposition exists, thereby proving R(3,3,3) >= 23.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The <3,3,3> tensor has a large symmetry group. If a rank-22 decomposition exists, it cannot preserve this symmetry group. Most automated and hand-constructed searches implicitly or explicitly restrict their search space to configurations that respect some subset of the tensor's symmetries to reduce the computational search space. If the only rank-22 decompositions lie in completely asymmetric orbits, these symmetry-reduced search classes will remain empty, causing the search to stall at 23.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
